title: Interfaces + Modules
story: You've mastered interfaces and you've mastered modules — now they combine. An interface defined in one module can be implemented by types in another module. The Logger interface lives in a `logging` module, but ConsoleLogger and FileLogger live in separate `backends` modules. Cross-module abstraction is the final boss of code organization.
why: Cross-module interfaces are the backbone of plugin architectures — the interface defines the contract, and implementations can live anywhere, even in separate modules that don't know about each other.
analogy: Cross-module interfaces are like USB standards — the USB specification (interface) is defined by one organization, but any company (module) can build a USB device (type) that implements it. Your computer (generic function) works with any USB device because they all follow the same standard. The computer doesn't need to know about every USB manufacturer.
try_it: Add a third backend: `push_notifier` module that 'notifies' by pushing to a Vec (simulating push notifications). Then build an `alert_system` module that takes a Vec of different notifiers and sends the same alert to ALL of them. Notice that each backend module is completely independent — you can add new backends without touching existing ones!
tips: Define interfaces in their OWN module — don't put the Logger interface in the console module
Backend modules import the interface module, never each other — they only know about the contract
The structural typing of XIOM means ANY module's type can satisfy ANY other module's interface — just have the method
common_mistakes: Defining the interface in the same module as one implementation — this couples the interface to that implementation
Forgetting to make the interface `pub` — interfaces are private by default and can't be used across modules
Accessing backend-specific fields in generic functions — `n.address` doesn't work; only interface methods are guaranteed
